meetings.title: Insights 2.0 launch planning
segments: Hi everyone. Ivy, can you hear us okay?
Yes, all good. Thanks for having me in on this, I've been looking forward to it.
Welcome, Ivy.
Thanks everyone. Ivy, welcome, great to have you on this.
The goal today is a draft launch plan I can bring to the alignment meeting. Nothing is final.
My starting point: I don't think we should do one big launch.
The model isn't at the quality bar yet.
I'd rather do a quiet private beta with design partners, and save the big moment for general availability.
What's the reason the model isn't ready?
I want to understand what I can and can't say in content.
Accuracy. When it groups feedback into themes, it's right about four times out of five today.
The goal is closer to nine out of ten before we call it generally available.
The beta is how we get there, because customers correcting it is what improves it.
Got it. So the beta content should be honest that it's early, and invite people to help shape it.
Exactly. 'Help us build it' is a good story in itself.
How long would the beta run before GA, roughly?
I need to plan my team's time.
It depends on the model, but I'd plan for six to eight weeks.
If the accuracy gets there faster, great.
If it takes longer, we extend the beta rather than rush GA.
Six to eight weeks with twenty partners is a lot of check-ins, but it's doable if we stagger them across the week.
And Andre starts soon, which helps with capacity.
I agree with that instinct.
A big launch with themes that are wrong a fifth of the time would be a bad first impression, and first impressions of AI features stick.
What about internal launch? Sales and CS need to know what's coming before customers hear about it.
Yes. I'd do an internal preview a week before the beta invites go out.
Demo, FAQ, and what you can and can't promise.
Especially no dates for GA.
Can the FAQ include what to say when a customer asks to join the beta and there's no room?
Yes. Something like: we're keeping it small so we can work closely with each team, and we'll let you know the moment it opens up.
And we add them to the waitlist, so nobody is forgotten.
Perfect. That's the question my team will get most.
And no promises about accuracy.
'It's early and it gets better as you use it' is the line.
From CS, a beta works well if it's a real program.
Regular check-ins, a shared channel, clear expectations.
Otherwise people sign up and never log in.
What would you want in the design partner agreement?
A simple one-pager, not a contract.
Weekly check-in, shared channel, a named person on their side, and permission to use anonymized feedback about the product.
And we ask up front if they'd be open to a case study at GA.
Keep it light. The moment it needs legal review, half of them will drop out.
How many partners could your team realistically support?
Around twenty. More than that and we can't talk to everyone weekly.
For GA, I'd build the launch around customer stories rather than features.
If we can get three strong stories from the beta, that's the backbone of the blog post, the webinar, and the sales deck.
What makes a customer story actually work, in your experience?
A specific moment. Not 'they saved time', but 'on a Monday in March, they noticed X, and because of that they did Y'.
Plus a number, and a named person who's willing to be quoted.
Without the named person, it reads like marketing.
Brightline would have been perfect for that, if they weren't so unhappy right now.
Maybe they still will be.
If the beta goes well for them, that's the best story of all.
How long does a good customer story take to produce?
About three weeks from interview to published, if the customer's approvals are quick.
Enterprise approvals can take longer.
So for GA, we'd want interviews to start about a month before.
That's useful for the calendar.
It means stories need to start during the beta, not after.
Tom, who could those stories come from?
Lakeshore Bank for sure. Their pilot feedback was glowing.
Probably a retail account too, and ideally a mid-market logistics or operations company.
Aisha has a good prospect there.
Would any of them do a video?
Video testimonials perform much better than written ones.
Lakeshore Bank, probably not, banks are careful.
A retail or logistics company, more likely.
I'll ask when I talk to them about the beta.
Let's not push video in the beta.
Ask for it at GA, once they've had a good experience.
What's the risk of asking beta customers for stories too early?
That they say yes to be polite, and then the product has a rough week and they regret it.
I'd wait until the fourth or fifth check-in.
By then you know who's genuinely happy.
That's a good rule. Stories from genuinely happy customers are always better.
I'll draft a content calendar that works backwards from GA.
Beta invite, a couple of teaser posts, stories, then the launch week.
Which channels would you focus on?
For the beta, mostly your own channels.
Customer newsletter, in-app announcement, and personal emails from Maya.
For GA, add the webinar, LinkedIn, and a couple of guest posts in CX communities where your buyers hang out.
The CX communities are a great idea.
That's where our best customers came from originally.
I'll include a list of the communities in the calendar, with who we know in each.
One caution. Don't put a GA date in anything public yet.
GA depends on the precision number, and I don't want us committed to a date the model can't hit.
What about a waitlist? Something public, so people can sign up for early access without a date?
I like that. It builds demand without committing to a date.
And it gives Aisha's team a reason to follow up with prospects.
As long as we don't promise waitlist people access in a specific time frame. Design partners first.
Understood. 'Be the first to know', not 'get access in two weeks'.
Understood. Everything relative to GA, no dates.
Okay, so the proposal for the alignment meeting is: private beta with about twenty design partners, run as a real program, and a story-led GA launch with no public date until precision is there.
One suggestion for the alignment meeting.
Lead with why two phases, before the what.
The engineers will be much more comfortable if they see we're not rushing the model.
Good idea. I'll open with the accuracy point, then the program, then the launch.
And I'll keep it to one page, since everyone's going to have a lot to read.
One page. Please.
Yes. Bring that. I'll make sure you have a slot.
I'll finalize the one-page plan before the alignment meeting.
And I'll start a list of story candidates.
Great. I think we have what we need.
Thanks everyone, and Ivy, I'll send you the brand guidelines after this.
Perfect. Looking forward to it.
Anything else before we wrap?
Just that I'd love to see the draft plan before the alignment meeting, so I'm not surprised by my own action items.
Ha, fair. I'll share it the day before.
Thanks everyone. Ivy, welcome aboard, this is going to be fun.
